extracted.intended_audience: forensic accountants, patent litigators, and professionals interested in patent damages and economic loss measurement
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining and applying the Panduit four-factor test for recovering lost-profits damages in U.S. patent infringement litigation, and the related debate over apportionment of damages. Includes discussion of recent case law (Mentor Graphics v. Synopsys) and possible Supreme Court review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of lost profits damages
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages represent the sales the patent owner would have earned but for the infringement, less variable costs (such as raw materials and labor) the owner would have incurred to earn those sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost-profits aim to put the patentee in the position they would have been absent infringement by measuring but-for sales and subtracting variable costs. This is the baseline economic concept underlying Panduit analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 1 — Demand for the patented product as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Demand for the patented product as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must establish there was market demand for the product at issue. The Federal Circuit has treated this requirement as tying damages to the product and its claimed features (see discussion of apportionment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 2 — Absence of acceptable non‑infringing alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: The absence of acceptable non-infringing alternatives (i.e., demand for particular features of the claimed invention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must show customers would not have purchased a non-infringing substitute instead; demonstrating demand for particular features helps link lost sales to the patented invention. Where acceptable substitutes exist, courts have sometimes allowed market-share based damages instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 3 — Manufacturing and marketing capabilities to exploit the demand
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturing and marketing capabilities to exploit the demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentee must have had the capacity and business organization to serve the lost sales (e.g., ability to manufacture, distribute, and market the product) so that but-for sales were feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panduit Factor 4 — The amount of profit it would have made but for the infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of profit it would have made but for the infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must quantify the profits that would have been earned on the but-for sales, accounting for appropriate costs (typically subtracting variable costs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Market-share damages when acceptable non‑infringing substitutes exist
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit has allowed patentees to recover damages based on market share when acceptable non-infringing substitutes were available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where proving lost sales attributable to the patented features is impractical because substitutes existed, courts may permit a market-share approach as an alternative measure of lost profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apportionment principle in lost-profits analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages must be commensurate with the value of the patented features; apportionment requires tying damages to specific claim limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court in Mentor Graphics found that the Panduit factors 'incorporate apportionment' because requiring demand for both the product as a whole and absence of non-infringing alternatives ties damages to the worth of patented features. This is the judiciary's method of ensuring lost-profits awards reflect the inventive contribution rather than the value of an entire multi-feature device.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejected two-step apportionment approach (defendant's proposal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Synopsys proposed a two-step process: (1) calculate the amount of profits lost from the infringement using the Panduit factors and (2) apportion its lost profits to cover only the patentee’s inventive contribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Federal Circuit rejected this separate two-step apportionment, concluding that Panduit already incorporates apportionment. The court did not, however, address whether alternative 'but for' damages theories could incorporate apportionment differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unresolved question: alternative 'but for' damages theories and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The court left open whether a different theory of 'but for' damages would adequately incorporate apportionment principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the panel found Panduit sufficient to satisfy apportionment principles in that case, it expressly declined to decide whether other lost‑profits methodologies might or might not meet apportionment requirements—a question potentially suitable for higher‑court review (e.g., U.S. Supreme Court).
